mad2-w4-q4.question: A Vue 3 child component contains this code. The parent renders `<TitleEditor title="Draft" />`. In a development build, what happens when `rename()` runs?

Fix: `const backup = [...this.items]` (a shallow copy is enough because the item objects themselves were not changed). Option A is the trap of assuming that storing it in a variable takes a snapshot.

mad2-w8-q1.question: A logged-in user (valid token) with the role "viewer" calls `DELETE /api/v1/projects/7`, which is allowed only for "admin". Which status code should the server send?
mad2-w8-q1.explanation: The user has been identified (the token is valid); their role simply lacks permission for this action. That is an authorisation failure: 403 Forbidden. Option A is a trap of naming: 401 "Unauthorized" is really for authentication failures, when the token is missing or invalid and the user must log in again. Option C is wrong because the request itself is well formed.

mad2-w8-q2.question: Which statement about the payload of a JWT signed (not encrypted) with HS256 is correct?
options: The payload is encrypted, so nobody can read it without the secret
The payload lives in the server database; the token holds only a random id
The signature hides the payload, so it is safe to put a password in it
The payload is only base64url-encoded; whoever holds the token can read it, so it should not contain secrets
mad2-w8-q2.explanation: The middle part of a JWT is a base64url encoding of JSON; anyone can decode it without the secret. The signature only lets you check that the header and payload were not changed (integrity); it does not hide them (no confidentiality). Options A and C are the trap of confusing encoding or signing with encryption; option B describes a session id, not a JWT.

mad2-w8-q3.question: JavaScript running on the page `https://app.example.com/dashboard` calls `fetch` on these URLs. Which request is cross-origin (needing CORS headers on the response)?
mad2-w8-q3.explanation: Origin = scheme + host + port. `api.example.com` and `app.example.com` are different hosts (sharing a parent domain does not make them the same origin), so option C is cross-origin. Option B is the trap of being thrown by the explicit port: 443 is the default HTTPS port, so the origin is the same. Options A and D differ only in path or query, which are not part of the origin.

mad2-w8-q4.question: An attacker changes `role` in the payload of their HS256 JWT from "editor" to "admin", base64url-encodes the new payload, and keeps the header and the old signature as they were. The server verifies the signature on every request. What happens?
options: The server rejects the token (401), because the signature is an HMAC of the header and payload; the HMAC of the new payload will not match the old signature, and a new signature cannot be made without the secret
The request runs as admin, because the payload is valid JSON and `exp` is still in the future
The server rejects it because the changed payload will not base64url-decode
The request works, but only as long as the user's old session cookie is also sent
mad2-w8-q4.explanation: The server recomputes `HMAC-SHA256(header + "." + payload, secret)` and compares it with the token's signature. Changing even one character of the payload changes the HMAC completely, and without the secret the attacker cannot produce a valid signature, so verification fails with 401. Option B is the trap of thinking the server just reads the payload and trusts it. Option C is wrong because the new payload is properly encoded too; what fails is the signature check, not decoding.

mad2-w8-q5.question: An app keeps a JWT access token with a 60-minute expiry in `localStorage`, and the server verifies the token only by signature and `exp` (no denylist). 10 minutes after logging in, the user logs out and the frontend deletes the token. But an XSS script had already stolen the token. Until when can the attacker use the API with it?
options: Access stops as soon as the user logs out
For roughly 50 more minutes, until the token expires
Forever, because a JWT never expires
Only while the user's browser tab is open
mad2-w8-q5.explanation: With stateless verification the server has nowhere to remember "this token was logged out"; the signature and `exp` are both valid, so the token works for 60 − 10 = 50 more minutes. Logging out only deleted the copy in the user's browser. Defences: short-lived access tokens + refresh tokens that can be revoked, a server-side denylist or token version, and keeping the token in an `HttpOnly` cookie so XSS cannot read it. Option A is the trap of confusing client-side logout with server-side revocation.

mad2-w8-q6.question: The frontend at `https://app.example.com` calls `fetch("https://api.example.com/me", { credentials: "include" })` (a simple GET). For CORS, the API response has only the header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`. What happens?
options: Everything works, because `*` allows every origin
The server rejects the request and sends 403

The request may reach the server, but the browser does not give the response to JavaScript (CORS error); with credentials the server must send the exact origin and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`
The browser automatically resends the request without cookies and returns that response
mad2-w8-q6.explanation: CORS rules are stricter for credentialed requests (with cookies): the wildcard `*` is not allowed, and the server must send both `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com` and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. A simple GET has no preflight, so the request can reach the server and be processed, but the browser hides the response from the page's JavaScript. Option A is the trap of reading `*` as "everything allowed"; option B is the trap of thinking CORS is applied by the server, when the browser enforces it.

mad2-w9-q1.question: A Flask endpoint builds a report that takes about 2 minutes. What is the best design for production?
options: Build the report inside the request and send the file with 200
Put the job on a task queue and immediately return 202 Accepted with a job id; the client polls a status endpoint
Raise the client and load-balancer timeouts to 5 minutes
Start a new thread inside the request and return 200 without a job id
mad2-w9-q1.explanation: 202 Accepted means "request received, the work will be completed later". With the job id the client can ask for status and result, and the work is done by workers that can be scaled separately. Option C is the trap of hiding the problem by raising timeouts: each long request would hold a server worker for 2 minutes. With option D there is no status, no retry, and the work is lost if the server restarts.

mad2-w9-q2.question: In a Celery-style background job system, what is the job of the broker (such as Redis or RabbitMQ)?
options: Storing the state and return value of each task
Distributing incoming web requests across servers
Holding task messages from the producer in a queue until a worker picks them up
mad2-w9-q2.explanation: The broker is a message queue: the web app puts task messages in and workers take them out, so the two run independently without waiting for each other. Option A is the job of the result backend (the same Redis can do both, which is why this confusion is common). Option B is done by workers, and option C is the load balancer's job.

mad2-w9-q3.question: A failing task is retried with exponential backoff: a 3 s wait before the first retry, and the wait doubles for each further retry. There are at most 5 retries. If every attempt fails, how much total waiting happens between the first failure and the start of the last attempt?
mad2-w9-q3.explanation: The waits for 5 retries are 3, 6, 12, 24, 48 s. Total = 3 + 6 + 12 + 24 + 48 = 93 s (that is, 3 × (2⁵ − 1)). Option A is the trap of taking only the last wait; option C is the trap of computing 3 × 2⁵ = 96 (one doubling too many); option D adds only 4 retries (3 + 6 + 12 + 24 = 45).

mad2-w9-q4.question: A Flask view has `send_invoice.delay(order)`, where `order` is a SQLAlchemy model object and Celery uses its default JSON serializer. What is the problem and the fix?
options: The model object will not serialize to JSON (an error), and even if another serializer sends it, the worker gets a stale snapshot from enqueue time; send `order.id` and let the worker read a fresh row from the DB
There is no problem; Celery passes the object to the worker just like a function call
The worker refreshes the object from the DB on its own, so it is just a little slower
It fails only with a Redis broker; it will work on RabbitMQ
mad2-w9-q4.explanation: The task message travels through the broker to another process (often another machine), so the arguments must be serialized; JSON does not understand a SQLAlchemy object. Even with a serializer like pickle, the worker would get a copy that is detached from any DB session and may be stale. Sending the id keeps the message small, and the worker always reads current data. Option B is the trap of treating `.delay()` as a normal function call; option D is the trap of blaming the broker for a serialization problem.

mad2-w9-q5.question: The task `charge_wallet(order_id)` deducts ₹500 from a user's wallet. The queue gives at-least-once delivery, so sometimes the same task runs twice. Which implementation is idempotent (only ₹500 is deducted even if it runs twice)?
options: `UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE user_id = ?`
Read the balance first, then write `balance - 500` back
In one transaction, insert a row into `payments` with `order_id` (UNIQUE), and deduct the balance only if the insert is new; do nothing on a duplicate
`sleep` for 1 second at the start of the task so that duplicate messages expire
mad2-w9-q5.explanation: The insert on a UNIQUE `order_id` detects the duplicate run: the second insert fails and the balance is not reduced again. Doing it in the same transaction also avoids a half state like "row inserted but money not deducted". Option A deducts 500 on every run: two runs = ₹1000. Option B also has a race condition and would deduct again on a duplicate. Option D is the trap of thinking duplicates are stopped by timing; a redelivery can happen at any time.

mad2-w9-q6.question: In a Celery beat schedule, a task is set to `crontab(minute="*/15", hour="9-17")` (a single beat instance, correct timezone). How many times a day is the task enqueued?
mad2-w9-q6.explanation: `hour="9-17"` includes both 9 and 17: 9 hours (9, 10, ..., 17). In each hour `*/15` means minutes 0, 15, 30, 45, so 4 runs. Total 9 × 4 = 36, the first at 09:00 and the last at 17:45. Option B is the trap of counting 17 − 9 = 8 hours (8 × 4 = 32); option A is the trap of thinking the schedule stops at 17:00 (32 + 1 = 33).

mad2-w10-q1.question: 3 different services (email, analytics, inventory) subscribe to the topic `order.created`. A separate work queue has 3 identical worker processes. One event is published to the topic and one job is put on the queue. How many times are the event and the job processed?
mad2-w10-q1.explanation: In pub/sub every subscriber gets its own copy of the event, so all three services process it: 3 times. Workers on a work queue are competing consumers: a message goes to only one worker, so the work is shared and not duplicated: 1 time. Option B is the trap of remembering the two models the wrong way round; option C is the trap of thinking a queue also gives every worker a copy.

mad2-w10-q2.question: A payment provider's webhook arrives. For each event you must build an invoice PDF and send an email, which takes ~30 s. The provider retries if it gets no answer within 10 s. What should the handler do?
options: Do the whole 30 s of work, then return 200
Return 500 first so that the provider resends later when the server is free
Ignore the webhook and poll the provider's API every minute
Verify the signature, store the event and enqueue a background job, and return 2xx immediately
mad2-w10-q2.explanation: The provider only needs to know that the event was received. Verify + store + enqueue takes milliseconds, and a worker builds the PDF and sends the email later. Option A is the trap of thinking it is "correct" to return 200 only once the work is done: after the 10 s timeout the provider retries and you get duplicate events. Option B deliberately creates retries and delay.

mad2-w10-q3.question: An Express webhook receiver already has a JSON body parser, and the code computes HMAC-SHA256 over `const body = JSON.stringify(req.body)` and compares it with the signature in the header. The secret is definitely right, yet most requests show a signature mismatch. What is the most likely cause?
options: SHA-256 gives a different output each time for the same input
The secret had to be base64-encoded first
The sender computed the HMAC over the raw bytes; parsing and re-stringifying can change whitespace, key order or number format, so the hash differs. Compute the HMAC over the raw body
HMAC signatures work only on GET requests
mad2-w10-q3.explanation: HMAC works on exact bytes: even one space of difference changes the whole digest. The body the sender sent (such as `"id": "evt_101"` with spaces) becomes `"id":"evt_101"` after `JSON.stringify`, so the receiver is hashing a different string. Verify over the raw body (for example with `express.raw()` or the parser's `verify` hook). Option A is the trap of treating hashing as random; SHA-256 is deterministic.

mad2-w10-q4.question: The consumer of an at-least-once queue is shown below. Because of network issues, some events were delivered again. What is the output?
mad2-w10-q4.explanation: The handler dedupes by event id: e1 (100) and e2 (50) were added the first time, the repeated e1 and e2 returned at `seen.has`, and e3 (25) was new. Total = 100 + 50 + 25 = 175, and the set holds 3 unique ids. Option A is the trap of treating every delivery as a new event (without dedupe it would be 350). Option D is the trap of thinking a `Set` also counts duplicate ids.

mad2-w10-q5.question: Despite HTTPS, an attacker somehow captures a valid signed webhook request (body + signature header) and resends it unchanged an hour later. The signature is an HMAC over the body only. What is the right way to prevent this replay attack?
options: Nothing can be done; if the signature is valid the request must be accepted
Include a timestamp in the signed content and have the receiver reject it when it is older than a tolerance window (such as 5 minutes); also dedupe by event id
HTTPS stops replay attacks by itself, so no other step is needed
Change the shared secret after every request
mad2-w10-q5.explanation: An HMAC over the body alone says nothing about when the request was made, so an old request still looks valid. If the timestamp is part of the signed content the attacker cannot change it (changing it breaks the signature), and the receiver rejects an hour-old request. Replays inside the window are caught by event-id dedupe. Option C is the trap of treating HTTPS (transport encryption) as replay protection; option D is not practical.

mad2-w10-q6.question: The order service consumes events that carry a version number. Because of retries, the events arrived in this order. What is the output?
mad2-w10-q6.explanation: The version starts at 1. "paid v2": 2 > 1, applied (applied = 1). "shipped v4": 4 > 2, applied (applied = 2). "packed v3": 3 ≤ 4, an old event, ignored; this is what stops the state going back from "shipped" to "packed". The second "paid v2": a duplicate, ignored. Final: shipped, version 4, applied 2. Option D is the trap of counting the late "packed" as applied too; option A is like applying the last arrival with no guard.

mad2-w11-q1.question: In SQLAlchemy the `author` relationship uses the default lazy loading, and each of the 50 posts has a different author. How many queries does this code send to the database?
mad2-w11-q1.explanation: The first query fetches 50 posts. In the loop, the first access to `p.author` runs a separate query for each post (the authors are all different, so no cache helps): 50 more. Total 1 + 50 = 51, which is the N+1 problem. Option A is what you get with `joinedload` (one query with a JOIN), option B with `selectinload` (posts + one `IN` query). Option C is the trap of forgetting to count the first query for the list.

mad2-w11-q2.question: An online banking account statement page is very sensitive; neither the browser nor any shared cache should store a copy of it at all. Which header is right?
mad2-w11-q2.explanation: `no-store` means the response must not be saved in any cache. Option A is a trap of naming: `no-cache` allows storing and only forces revalidation with the server before each reuse, so a copy can stay on disk. Option B also treats the response as immediately stale and forces revalidation, but does not stop storing. Option D is a year of public caching, the exact opposite of what sensitive data needs.

mad2-w11-q3.question: An API endpoint has 10 response times (ms): 120, 95, 110, 105, 900, 100, 115, 98, 102, 1200. Use the nearest-rank method (position ⌈p/100 × n⌉ in the sorted list). What are p50, p90 and the mean?
mad2-w11-q3.explanation: Sorted: 95, 98, 100, 102, 105, 110, 115, 120, 900, 1200 (n = 10). p50: position ⌈0.5 × 10⌉ = 5, value 105. p90: position ⌈0.9 × 10⌉ = 9, value 900. Mean = 2945 / 10 = 294.5. Two slow requests pushed the mean to about 3 times the median, which is why latency is read in percentiles. Option B is the trap of counting one position too far (6th and 10th), and option C swaps the mean and the median.

mad2-w11-q4.question: In steady state a service handles 200 requests/second with an average latency of 150 ms. By Little's law, how many requests are inside the system (in flight) at a time on average?
mad2-w11-q4.explanation: L = λ × W = 200 req/s × 0.150 s = 30. Match the units: ms must be converted to seconds. Option A is the trap of computing 200 / 0.150 (dividing), and option D is the trap of taking 150 ms as 1.5 s. This means you need at least ~30 concurrent workers/connections, or requests will wait in a queue and push latency up further.

mad2-w11-q5.question: With the cache-aside pattern, a product price was cached at t = 0 s (value ₹999, TTL 300 s). At t = 120 s an admin changes the price in the DB to ₹899, but the cache key is not deleted. What do reads at t = 200 s and t = 310 s return?
mad2-w11-q5.explanation: At t = 200 the cache entry is still valid (it expires at 300), so it is a cache hit: the old ₹999 (stale). At t = 310 the entry has expired, so it is a miss, the new ₹899 comes from the DB and is cached again. Option A is the trap of thinking a DB update reaches the cache by itself; without invalidation the stale window can be as long as the TTL. That is why you do `DEL key` on write.

mad2-w11-q6.question: A feed API returns posts newest-first with `ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET ?`. The user has seen page 1 (OFFSET 0) and page 2 (OFFSET 20). Now 5 new posts are created, and then the user opens page 3 (OFFSET 40). How many posts on page 3 were already shown on page 2?
mad2-w11-q6.explanation: The 5 new posts go on top, so every old post moves 5 positions down. Page 2 was positions 21–40; now OFFSET 40 gives positions 41–60, which hold the old 36–55. The old 36–40 were already shown on page 2: 5 repeats (and in the other direction an item can be missed when rows are deleted). Keyset pagination (`WHERE created_at < :last_seen`) continues after the last item seen, so 0 repeats. Option A is the trap of assuming OFFSET is stable.

mad2-w12-q1.question: In a Vue + Flask app, only admins may delete projects. Where must this rule really be enforced?
options: Only in the frontend: hide the delete button for non-admins
Only in the Vue Router `beforeEach` guard
On the server in the DELETE endpoint (role check); hiding the button in the frontend is only for UX
In the `isAdmin` flag of the Pinia store
mad2-w12-q1.explanation: All code running in the browser is under the user's control: they can change the store in DevTools, skip the guard, or call the API directly with `curl`. So authorisation happens on the server, where the role (and ownership) is checked as the request arrives. Options A, B and D are the trap of treating UX checks as security; they are good, but they only spare the user from seeing the wrong button.

mad2-w12-q2.question: What does this code print?
mad2-w12-q2.explanation: `map` doubles each element: [6, 2, 4]. `filter` keeps only values greater than 2: [6, 4] (2 > 2 is false). `reduce` adds them from 0: 6 + 4 = 10. Option A is the trap of skipping the filter (6 + 2 + 4 = 12); option D is the trap of forgetting `reduce` and writing the filter result.

mad2-w12-q3.question: In what order are the lines printed?
options: a1 → b → s → a2 → p → t
a1 → b → a2 → s → p → t
a1 → s → b → p → a2 → t
a1 → b → s → t → a2 → p
mad2-w12-q3.explanation: `placeOrder()` prints "a1" synchronously and calls `save()` right away: "b". At `await` the function pauses and the "a2" part goes into the microtask queue. Then `Promise.resolve().then` queues "p" behind that microtask, and "s" is printed synchronously. Microtasks run in FIFO order: "a2", then "p". Finally the timer task "t". Option B is the trap of thinking `await` does not pause because `save()` is synchronous; option D is the trap of running the timer before the microtasks.

mad2-w12-q4.question: Users upload videos of up to 2 GB that must be transcoded into several resolutions (several minutes per video). With the tools from this course, what is the best design?
options: Transcode inside the upload request and return 200 when done
Transcode in the browser with JavaScript and upload all the files
Keep the upload request open and have the frontend poll every second to see whether it has finished
Save the file to object storage, enqueue a Celery task and return 202 + job id; a worker transcodes and updates the status, and the frontend polls or gets a notification
mad2-w12-q4.explanation: Several minutes of CPU-heavy work does not fit in the request-response cycle: timeouts and tied-up web workers. After the upload the file goes to storage, and only the file key goes in the task arguments, not the big data in the broker. The worker transcodes at its own pace, retries are possible, and workers scale separately. Option A is the trap of calling the synchronous design "simple"; option C keeps the same timeout problem with an open request.

mad2-w12-q5.question: The Settings page changes the name with `PUT /api/v1/me`; the server returns 200 with the updated user JSON, and the Settings component keeps it in its own local `ref`. The navbar shows the name from `user.name` in the Pinia `auth` store. Why does the navbar show the old name until the page is reloaded?
options: The browser cached the PUT response
Data in a Pinia store is not reactive
The response went only into the Settings local `ref`; the store's `user` was never updated. Do the update through an auth store action that sets `this.user` from the response
The JWT expired as soon as the name changed
mad2-w12-q5.explanation: The navbar reads the store, and no new data ever reached the store: Settings kept the result to itself, so the shared state now has two separate "truths". On reload the store fetches a fresh user from the server, which is why it looks right then. Fix: change shared data through a store action, so every component that reads it updates automatically. Option B has it backwards: the store is reactive, the problem is that it was never changed. Option A is wrong because browsers do not cache PUT responses.

mad2-w12-q6.question: At peak, 200 report jobs arrive per minute and each job occupies one worker process for 4 s (one process handles one job at a time). At least how many worker processes are needed to stop the queue from growing without bound?
mad2-w12-q6.explanation: Arrival rate = 200 / 60 ≈ 3.33 jobs/s. By Little's law the jobs running at once ≈ 3.33 × 4 ≈ 13.33. There is no such thing as a fraction of a worker, and 13 workers can finish only 13 / 4 = 3.25 jobs/s, which is below 3.33, so round up to 14. Option B is the trap of rounding down; option C computes 200 / 4 (mixing per minute with seconds); option D computes 200 × 4.

mad2-w1-q7.question: What does this code print?
mad2-w1-q7.explanation: `||` falls back on every falsy value, so `0 || 5` → 5. `??` falls back only on `null`/`undefined`: `0 ?? 5` → 0 (0 is a valid value), and `null ?? 5` → 5. Option A's trap is treating `??` like `||`; option C thinks `||` would also keep 0; option D forgets that `null ?? 5` applies the default.

mad2-w1-q8.question: Which of these values counts as truthy in `if (value)`?
mad2-w1-q8.explanation: The list of falsy values is short: `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN`. `"0"` is a non-empty string, so it is truthy even though it contains a zero. The trap is treating `"0"` like the number 0; `0`, `""` and `NaN` are all on the falsy list.

mad2-w1-q9.question: What does this code print?
mad2-w1-q9.explanation: All numbers are 64-bit floating point: 0.1 + 0.2 actually gives 0.30000000000000004, so `=== 0.3` is false. JavaScript has no separate integer division, so 7 / 2 = 3.5. Option A treats decimal maths as exact; options B and C assume integer division (3), which you only get with `Math.floor` or `Math.trunc`.

mad2-w1-q10.question: What does this code print?
mad2-w1-q10.explanation: `===` compares objects by reference: two separate `[1]` literals are two different arrays, so false. `Array.isArray([])` is true, and `typeof []` gives "object" because an array is an object too. The trap in options B and C is treating `[1] === [1]` as a value comparison; options B and D expect "array" from `typeof`.

mad2-w1-q11.question: What does this code print?
mad2-w1-q11.explanation: `var` is function-scoped (global here), so `var a = 2` inside the block reassigns the same `a`: outside, `a` is 2. `let b = 2` creates a new, separate `b` inside the block that ends with the block, so the outer `b` stays 1. Option B thinks `let` also leaks out like `var`; option A treats `var` as block-scoped; option D is wrong because declaring `let` again in a different block is allowed.

mad2-w1-q12.question: What does this code print?
mad2-w1-q12.explanation: `f1` is a function declaration, which is hoisted in full: "function". `f2` is a `var`, hoisted and initialised to `undefined`; the function is assigned only on its later line: "undefined". `f3` is a `const` still in the TDZ; inside the TDZ even `typeof` throws a `ReferenceError`, which the `catch` captures. Option C's trap is thinking `typeof` is always safe; option B treats function expressions as fully hoisted too; option D does not hoist even the declaration.

mad2-w1-q13.question: What does this code print?
mad2-w1-q13.explanation: Work left to right. (1) `"3" * "4"`: `*` turns both into numbers = 12; then in `12 + "1"` one side is a string, so "121". (2) `1 + 2` = 3 (both numbers), then `3 + "3"` = "33". (3) `"1" + 2` = "12" (a string), then `"12" + 3` = "123". Option A assumes numeric addition everywhere; option C assumes concatenation from the start in the second expression; option D treats `+ "1"` in the first expression as adding a number.

mad2-w1-q14.question: What does this code print?
mad2-w1-q14.explanation: Spread makes a shallow copy: changing `s.name` does not change `orig.name` ("Asha"), but `s.marks` and `orig.marks` are the same array, so after pushing 90 `orig.marks` has length 3. `structuredClone` is a deep copy that made its own copy of [70, 80] at the start; pushing 100 into it gives length 3. Option C treats spread as a deep copy; option B assumes `d` shares the same array too; option A thinks changing `s.name` also changes the original.

mad2-w1-q15.question: What does this code print?
mad2-w1-q15.explanation: `a`: `v == null` is true only for `null` and `undefined` = 2. `b`: the falsy values `0`, `""`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN` = 5 (`"0"` is truthy). `c`: with `== 0`, `0`, `""` (it becomes the number 0) and `"0"` are true; `null == 0` is false by the special rule, and `undefined` and `NaN` are false too = 3. Option B leaves `undefined` out of `== null`; option C counts `"0"` as falsy; option D also counts `null` and `undefined` as `== 0`.

mad2-w2-q7.question: What does this code print?
mad2-w2-q7.explanation: `filter` keeps only the even numbers: [2, 4]. Then `map` multiplies each by 10: [20, 40], and `join` makes "20,40". Option A keeps the odd numbers; option C forgets the `map` step; option D assumes `filter` removes nothing.

mad2-w2-q8.question: What does this code print?
options: TypeError: Cannot read properties of null
mad2-w2-q8.explanation: As soon as `?.` meets `null` or `undefined` in the middle, the whole expression gives `undefined` instead of an error. `u.profile` is null, so `u.profile?.city` → `undefined` (not null). `u.settings` does not exist, so `u.settings?.theme` → `undefined`. Every change must first `commit` a mutation, not go through an action
Store state can only be changed inside getters, not in actions
After changing state the component must reload the page before it shows
mad2-w7-q7.explanation: In Pinia, actions are normal methods that can change state directly through `this`; there is no need for separate mutations as in Vuex. Option B is a Vuex rule, not a Pinia one; option C is wrong because getters are for derived values, not for changing state; option D has nothing to do with reactivity.

mad2-w7-q8.question: Why should mutations in Vuex be synchronous?
options: Because async functions in JavaScript cannot change objects at all
So devtools can keep an exact before/after record of every state change
Because mutations run on the server, not in the browser
So that getters are never cached and are always recalculated
mad2-w7-q8.explanation: Vuex tracks every `commit` as a record so devtools can show the before/after snapshot of the state. If a mutation has an `await` inside, the real change happens after it was recorded and the history is wrong. So async work goes in actions, and only the final change goes in a mutation. Options A, C and D are false facts.

mad2-w7-q9.question: After a logout, the next user logs in on the same browser and sees the previous user's cart (a Pinia options store). What is the most direct fix?
options: Save the cart in `localStorage` as well
Create a new store in each component instead of `useCartStore()`
Call `$reset()` on the user-specific stores at logout
mad2-w7-q9.explanation: The store is one in-memory instance for the whole app, so the previous user's cart stays after logout. In an options store, `$reset()` brings the state back to the initial object from the `state()` function. Option A makes the problem worse (the data would survive a reload too); option B is wrong because `useCartStore()` always returns the same instance; option D only hides the data, it does not clear it.

mad2-w7-q10.question: A component needs both the Pinia store's `count` (it must stay reactive) and the action `increment`. Which code is correct?
mad2-w7-q10.explanation: `storeToRefs` gives refs for state and getters, but leaves out actions; so in option A `increment` is undefined. In option B `count` is a plain copy that never updates. Option C makes both mistakes at once. Correct: state through `storeToRefs` and the action straight from the store, because Pinia keeps actions bound to the store.

mad2-w7-q11.question: What do the `subtotal` and `total` getters give in this Pinia store?
mad2-w7-q11.explanation: `subtotal` = 120 × 2 + 45 × 4 = 240 + 180 = 420. In `total`, 420 > 400, so 420 − 40 = 380. Option A adds only the prices (120 + 45) and forgets the qty; option B misses the discount condition; option C applies the discount twice.

mad2-w7-q12.question: Two versions of a Pinia optimistic delete are written as simplified JavaScript; in both, the rollback runs because the API failed. What is the output?
mad2-w7-q12.explanation: Variant P: `backup` points to the old array, and `filter` creates a new array; the old one was never touched, so after the rollback 1,2,3 is back. Variant Q: `backup` and `items.list` are the same array, and `splice` changes that array in place, so the backup became 1,3 as well; the rollback brings nothing back. Option B assumes `const backup = ...` makes a copy; option A assumes `filter` also changes the original; option D gets both backwards. Fix: `const backup = [...items.list]`.

mad2-w7-q13.question: This is a small simplified Vuex-like store (mutation `add`, async action `addLater`). What is the output?
mad2-w7-q13.explanation: `addLater(5)` starts synchronously and reads `before` = 0 before the `await`. Then the action pauses, and the next line `commit("add", 2)` sets count to 2 immediately. 100 ms later the action does `commit("add", 5)`: 7, and returns `before` (0). Option A assumes `before` was read after commit 2; option C forgets commit 2; option D takes `before` to be the final value.

mad2-w7-q14.question: In this Pinia store, what does the `total` getter give before and after `update()`?
mad2-w7-q14.explanation: Before: `subtotal` = 300 × 2 + 150 × 1 = 750; the coupon is "SAVE10", so `discount` = 75; `total` = 675. `update()` removes the coupon and sets the second line's qty to 3: `subtotal` = 600 + 450 = 1050, `discount` = 0, `total` = 1050. Getters recalculate when their dependencies change. Option B forgets the discount in the first case; option C still takes 10% off after the coupon is removed; option D adds the discount instead of subtracting it.

mad2-w7-q15.question: This code runs in a component (the store is shown below). What is the output?
mad2-w7-q15.explanation: `const { n } = store` is a plain copy of a primitive: it stays 1. `inc()` twice: `store.n` = 1 + 2 + 2 = 5. `double` is a ref from `storeToRefs`, so `double.value` gives the fresh getter value: 5 × 2 = 10. Destructuring the action is fine because Pinia keeps it bound to the store. Option A treats `n` as reactive; option B treats the getter's ref as a frozen copy too; option C assumes a destructured action cannot change the store.

mad2-w8-q7.question: `POST /api/v1/projects` creates a new project. Which status code fits success best?
mad2-w8-q7.explanation: When a new resource is created, the REST convention is `201 Created`, usually with the new resource's JSON body. `204` is for success with no body (such as a DELETE); `301` is for a redirect and `404` is for "resource not found".

mad2-w8-q8.question: Which of these is an example of authorisation (not authentication)?
options: Checking the user's password, logging them in and giving a session
Confirming the user's identity by sending and verifying an OTP
Checking before a delete that the logged-in user's role is "admin"
Working out from the session id cookie which user a request belongs to
mad2-w8-q8.explanation: Authentication = "who you are" (identifying the user from a password, OTP or session cookie). Authorisation = "what you may do": checking the role to allow or deny a delete. Options A, B and D are all about identity, that is, authentication.

mad2-w8-q9.question: What is the effect of setting the `HttpOnly` flag on a session cookie?
options: The cookie is sent only over HTTPS connections
The cookie is not sent with cross-site requests
The cookie stays forever, even after the browser is closed
JavaScript (`document.cookie`) cannot read it; protects against XSS
mad2-w8-q9.explanation: `HttpOnly` hides the cookie from JavaScript (it does not appear in `document.cookie`), so an XSS script cannot steal the session id; the cookie still goes to the server with every request. Sending only over HTTPS is what `Secure` does (option A), blocking it on cross-site requests is `SameSite` (option B), and expiry has nothing to do with `HttpOnly` (option C).

mad2-w8-q10.question: The page runs on `https://app.example.com`. Before which of these requests does the browser send an `OPTIONS` preflight?
options: `fetch("https://api.example.com/items")` (a simple GET, no custom headers, no body)
`` loading on the page (a cross-origin image)
mad2-w8-q10.explanation: A preflight happens only for cross-origin requests, and only when the request is not "simple": a PUT/DELETE method, a JSON `Content-Type` or an `Authorization` header. Option B is a PUT with a JSON header to a different host (`api.example.com`), so there is a preflight. Option A has DELETE and a JSON header but is same-origin, so CORS does not apply at all; option C is cross-origin but a simple GET (no preflight, only a CORS header on the response is needed); option D is not a `fetch`, it is a normal image load.

mad2-w8-q11.question: A mobile app uses the `name` field in the response of `/api/v1/users`. Which of these changes is breaking and should go into `/api/v2`?
options: Adding a new optional field `avatar_url` to the response
mad2-w8-q11.explanation: Renaming a field breaks old clients that read `name`, so it is a breaking change and goes into a new version. Adding a new optional field or a new endpoint does not break old clients (options A, B), and compression is transparent at the HTTP level (option C).

mad2-w8-q12.question: A JWT's payload is `{"sub": "u7", "role": "editor", "iat": 1767225600, "exp": 1767226500}` (Unix seconds). How long is the token valid, and what happens to a request with this token at server time 1767226800?
options: 15 minutes; the request is rejected (401), because `exp` passed 300 s ago
15 minutes; the request goes through because the signature is valid
mad2-w8-q12.explanation: Validity = `exp` − `iat` = 1767226500 − 1767225600 = 900 s = 15 minutes. The request time is 300 s past `exp`, and the server must check `exp`, so the token has expired: 401 (authentication failed). Option B treats the signature as enough; option C reads seconds as minutes; option D mistakes the 300 s for the validity, and 403 is the wrong code too (this is an identity failure, not a permission one).

mad2-w8-q13.question: The Flask endpoint `PATCH /api/v1/documents/<id>` has only `@roles_required("editor")`. User 12 (role "editor") sends a PATCH for document 88, whose owner is user 30. What happens, and what is the right fix?
options: A 403, because the role decorator also checks the owner; no fix needed
The update goes through (IDOR bug); check in the endpoint that the document's owner is the current user, else 403
A 401, because user 12's token was not issued for document 88
The update goes through, and that is fine because the frontend hides the edit button on other people's documents
mad2-w8-q13.explanation: The decorator checks only the role, and user 12 is an editor, so the request passes: someone else's document was edited just by changing the id (IDOR bug). Fix: in the endpoint, load the document and check that `doc.owner_id == current_user.id` (or that the user is an admin), else 403. Option A assumes the role check also looks at ownership; option C is wrong because a token identifies the user and is not issued per document; option D treats hiding things in the frontend as security.

mad2-w8-q14.question: The Vue dev server is on `http://localhost:5173` and Flask is on `http://localhost:5000`. The frontend calls `fetch("http://localhost:5000/api/tasks", { method: "POST", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body })`. Flask answers the `OPTIONS` request with a 404 and no CORS headers. What does the browser do?
options: Sends only the POST, because the same-origin policy and CORS do not apply on localhost
Sends both OPTIONS and POST, but does not show the POST response to JavaScript
Sends OPTIONS first; since it fails, the POST is never sent and `fetch` rejects with a CORS error
When OPTIONS fails, the browser re-sends the POST in `no-cors` mode by itself
mad2-w8-q14.explanation: `5173` and `5000` are different ports, so the origin is different (CORS applies on localhost too). A POST with a JSON `Content-Type` is not a simple request, so the browser sends an `OPTIONS` preflight first. The preflight response has no CORS headers (404), so the browser never sends the real POST and `fetch` rejects with a CORS error. Option A treats localhost as an exception; option B assumes the POST still goes out after a failed preflight; option D: there is no such automatic retry.

mad2-w8-q15.question: The access token lasts 15 minutes (the server checks only the signature + `exp`, no denylist), and the refresh token is in an `HttpOnly` cookie that can be revoked server-side. The user logs in at 10:00 (the access token was issued at 10:00). At 10:05 an XSS script steals the access token from `localStorage`. At 10:06 the user logs out and the server revokes the refresh token. Until when can the attacker use the API?
options: Until 10:15, when the stolen access token expires
Until 10:06, access ends as soon as the user logs out
For ever, by making new access tokens with the refresh token
mad2-w8-q15.explanation: The access token is stateless: the server only looks at the signature and `exp`, so logging out or revoking the refresh token does not stop the stolen access token. It was issued at 10:00 and lasts 15 minutes, so it works until 10:15. The refresh token was in an `HttpOnly` cookie, which XSS cannot read, and it was revoked as well, so the attacker cannot make new tokens. Option B treats a stateless JWT like a session; option C counts the expiry from the time of the theft; option D assumes the attacker also has the refresh token.

mad2-w9-q7.question: A Flask view has `job = build_report.delay(user_id, month)`. What does this line do?
options: Queues the message and at once returns an `AsyncResult` (with the job `id`); a worker runs it
Holds the request until the report is built and then returns the report's full result
Runs the task to completion right away in the same request thread, then moves on
Adds the task to the Celery beat schedule for the next day, so it will not run today
mad2-w9-q7.explanation: `.delay(...)` is a shortcut for `apply_async`: the message goes to the broker and you get an `AsyncResult` at once, so the endpoint can return 202 + a job id. A separate worker process does the work. Options B and C describe synchronous behaviour; option D is scheduling (beat), not what `delay` does.

mad2-w9-q8.question: What does Celery beat do?
options: Executing scheduled tasks itself in its own process, instead of the workers
Enqueuing the task when its time comes; the workers still run it
Storing and keeping every task's result and state in Redis
Finding failed tasks in the dead-letter queue and removing them
mad2-w9-q8.explanation: Beat is only a scheduler: for example at `crontab(minute=0, hour=18)` it puts the task message on the queue when the time comes. Workers execute it (option A is wrong), storing results is the result backend's job (option C), and the dead-letter queue has nothing to do with beat (option D).

mad2-w9-q9.question: On which of these errors is retrying the task with backoff the right call?
options: 400 Bad Request, because the input sent was wrong
Validation error: the email field is empty
A 503 or a network timeout from a third-party API
404: the given user id does not exist
mad2-w9-q9.explanation: Retrying only helps with transient errors: a 503 or a timeout may clear up after a while. A 400, a validation error or a missing user (options A, B, D) will not change by running again; a retry only adds load, so mark it FAILURE straight away and report it.

mad2-w9-q10.question: The frontend polls `GET /api/jobs/abc123`, but the id `abc123` was never enqueued (a typo). What does Celery's `AsyncResult("abc123").state` show?
mad2-w9-q10.explanation: Celery returns PENDING even for an unknown job id, because having no entry in the result backend can also mean "not started yet". So record job ids in your own DB and return 404 for an unknown id. Options A, B and C wrongly assume Celery recognises an unknown id.

mad2-w9-q11.question: A task in Celery beat is set to `crontab(minute=30, hour="*/6")`. How many times a day is it enqueued?
options: 24 times: at minute 30 of every hour
mad2-w9-q11.explanation: `hour="*/6"` means every 6 hours: 0, 6, 12, 18, that is 4 hours a day, and `minute=30` fires once in each of those hours. 4 in total. Option A reads the step as a count; option C ignores `hour`; option D reads `*/6` as "only at 6 o'clock".

mad2-w9-q12.question: A task's retry delays are `min(3 × 2ⁿ, 30)` seconds (n = retries so far, starting at 0), and `max_retries` is 6. If every attempt fails, what is the total wait across all the retries?
mad2-w9-q12.explanation: For n = 0 to 5: 3, 6, 12, 24, then the cap of 30 instead of 48, and 30 instead of 96 too. Total = 3 + 6 + 12 + 24 + 30 + 30 = 105 s. Option A forgets the cap (3 + 6 + ... + 96 = 189); option B counts only 5 retries without the cap (93); option C adds one extra retry (105 + 30 = 135).

mad2-w9-q13.question: 30 tasks are put on the queue at once (FIFO order). There are 3 workers, each runs one task at a time, and each task takes 4 s. When does task #20 finish, and when are all the tasks done?
mad2-w9-q13.explanation: The 3 workers finish 3 tasks in each 4 s round. Task #20 is in round ⌈20 / 3⌉ = 7 (tasks 19–21), which starts at t = 24 s and ends at 28 s. 30 tasks = 10 rounds = 40 s. Option B counts as if there were one worker (20 × 4, 30 × 4); option C gives task #20's start time; option D counts one round too few (9 × 4).

mad2-w9-q14.question: This consumer takes tasks from an at-least-once queue, and the third delivery is a duplicate of `o1`. What is the output?
mad2-w9-q14.explanation: The bug is that stock is reduced before the duplicate check. o1: stock 8, email 1. o2: stock 7, email 2. o1 again: stock drops to 5, then the duplicate is caught, so no email. Output 5 2. Option A assumes the check blocks everything (that would be true if it were the first line); option B assumes there is no dedupe at all; option D gets the stock right but counts the email twice.

mad2-w9-q15.question: The user starts with 100 points. `notify_crm` times out on the first 2 attempts and works on the third. When the task finishes, what are the user's points and the task's state?
mad2-w9-q15.explanation: Every retry runs the whole task function from the start. The UPDATE comes before the retry line and has already been committed, so every attempt adds 10: 3 attempts = 100 + 30 = 130. The third attempt succeeds and 2 retries is under `max_retries` (5), so the state is SUCCESS. Option A assumes a retry reruns only the failed line; option B treats retries as failure; option C assumes a failed attempt rolls back its DB work. Fix: make the work idempotent (for example, give the points only once per unique sync id) or move the CRM call to a separate task.

mad2-w10-q7.question: The order service publishes events on the `order.created` topic. Now a new "loyalty points" service also wants to act on every order. What has to be done with pub/sub?
options: The loyalty service subscribes to the topic; the order service's code does not change
A direct HTTP call to the loyalty service must be added to the order service
The email service must also do the loyalty points work
The topic must be turned into a point-to-point queue
mad2-w10-q7.explanation: In pub/sub every subscriber gets its own copy of the event, so a new consumer simply subscribes; the producer does not even notice. Option B is the very synchronous coupling we wanted to avoid; option C mixes up the services' responsibilities; option D is backwards, because in a queue each message goes to only one consumer.

mad2-w10-q8.question: What is a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for?
options: Keeping a permanent backup copy of every message
Setting aside messages that keep failing (poison messages)
Deleting old messages that are already processed
Storing messages encrypted in the broker
mad2-w10-q8.explanation: If a poison message (one that fails every time) keeps cycling through the queue, the other messages get stuck. The DLQ moves it aside after a few attempts, so someone can inspect it and the rest of the queue keeps flowing. Options A, C and D are not what a DLQ does.

mad2-w10-q9.question: A consumer acknowledges every message before it starts processing it. Which delivery guarantee is this?
options: At-least-once: duplicates may come, but nothing is lost
At-most-once: no duplicates, but a message can be lost on a crash
Ordered delivery: messages always in the right order
mad2-w10-q9.explanation: Acking first means the broker considers the message delivered and forgets it. If the consumer crashes mid-processing, the message will not come again (it is lost), but there are never duplicates either. Option B is what happens when the ack comes after processing; option A is very hard in distributed systems and does not come from ack timing alone; option D, ordering, is a separate guarantee.

mad2-w10-q10.question: What is the real reason to compare a webhook signature with `crypto.timingSafeEqual` instead of `===`?
options: `===` cannot compare two strings byte by byte at all
`timingSafeEqual` decrypts the hash and matches it with the original
`timingSafeEqual` is faster than `===`, so there is less load
Equal time on every byte; the signature cannot be guessed from response time
mad2-w10-q10.explanation: `===` stops at the first differing character, so the response time for a wrong signature hints at how many leading characters were right; with many requests an attacker can guess the signature piece by piece. A constant-time compare always checks the full length. Option A is wrong (`===` does compare strings); option B: an HMAC is not decrypted; option C: speed is not the reason.

mad2-w10-q11.question: A queue holds 1200 messages, each takes 0.5 s to process, and there are 4 competing consumers (each handles one message at a time). Roughly how long until the queue is empty?
mad2-w10-q11.explanation: Competing consumers share the work: each consumer gets 1200 ÷ 4 = 300 messages, × 0.5 s = 150 s. Option A is the time for a single consumer (1200 × 0.5); option C assumes 2 consumers instead of 4; option D multiplies by the number of consumers instead of dividing (600 × 4).

mad2-w10-q12.question: This is a webhook receiver's simplified accept logic (timestamp tolerance 300 s). What is the output?
mad2-w10-q12.explanation: Call 1: signature ok, age 1767225900 − 1767225800 = 100 s ≤ 300, new id: "ok". Call 2: age 400 s > 300: "stale". Call 3: wrong signature, the very first check gives "bad-sig". Call 4: age 50 s, but `e1` was already seen: "dup". Option A forgets the stale check; option B forgets the dedupe; option D ignores `sigOk` being false.

mad2-w10-q13.question: A topic has 3 subscriber groups: email (2 instances, competing), analytics (1 instance) and inventory (3 instances, competing). 10 events are published. How many event processings happen in total, and how many events do the two email instances process between them?
mad2-w10-q13.explanation: Every subscriber group gets one copy of each event, and the instances inside a group are competing consumers (only one of them processes each copy). 10 events × 3 groups = 30 processings. The email group gets 10 copies, shared between its two instances: 10 between them. Option B treats every instance as a separate subscriber (10 × 6); option C forgets the fan-out; option D gives every event to each email instance.

mad2-w10-q14.question: A consumer reads 5 messages (m1 to m5) in order and acks each one before it starts processing it. It crashes in the middle of processing m3 and then restarts. In the end, which messages were fully processed?
options: All of m1–m5, because m3 will be delivered again
Only m1 and m2; the queue stops for good after the crash
m1, m2, m4, m5; m3 was lost (it had already been acked)
mad2-w10-q14.explanation: This is an at-most-once setup: m3 was acked before the crash, so the broker will not send it again, and its half-done work is lost. After the restart the consumer takes m4 and m5. Options A and B are at-least-once (ack after processing) behaviour; option C is wrong, the remaining messages are delivered after the restart.

mad2-w10-q15.question: What does this code print? (The secret is for the demo only.)
mad2-w10-q15.explanation: An HMAC with the same secret and the same input always gives the same output: the first is true. Changing the timestamp by one second changes the signed string and the hash is completely different: false. The third: this raw body has no extra spaces and its keys are in the same order, so `JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(raw))` produces exactly the same string: true. Option A's trap is memorising that parse + stringify always breaks the signature (it does when spaces, key order or number format change, which is why verifying the raw bytes is the safe rule); option B assumes the timestamp is not part of the signed content; option C treats HMAC as random.

mad2-w11-q7.question: In latency metrics, what does p50 tell you?
options: The median: half the requests are faster than it and half slower
The average response time of the slowest 50 requests
The percent of all requests that take under 50 ms
The plain average (mean) of all the requests
mad2-w11-q7.explanation: p50 is the 50th percentile, that is, the median: the typical user's experience. It is different from the mean, because a few very slow requests skew the mean but not the median (option D). Options B and C attach the "50" to the wrong thing.

mad2-w11-q8.question: A Vite build produces `index.html` and content-hashed files (such as `app.3f9a1c.js`). Which header suits `index.html` best so that a new deploy shows up immediately?
options: No header; the browser will work it out
mad2-w11-q8.explanation: `index.html` keeps the same name on every deploy, so give it `no-cache`: the browser may store it but revalidates with the ETag every time, and a new deploy arrives at once. The year-long `immutable` (option A) is only for hashed files, whose names change when their content changes; option C can show old HTML for up to a day; with option D the browser may cache it by its own guesswork.

mad2-w11-q9.question: `GET /api/me` returns the logged-in user's name and email, and the app sits behind a CDN. Which header should this response have?
options: `Cache-Control: private` (or `no-store`) so the CDN does not share it
No header; the CDN spots personal data in the response by itself
mad2-w11-q9.explanation: If a personalised response lands in a shared cache (the CDN), the next user may get someone else's data. `private` lets only the user's own browser cache it; for very sensitive data use `no-store`. Options A and B allow long shared caching and can leak data; option D: a CDN does not understand what a response means, it only follows the headers.

mad2-w11-q10.question: An API gets 2000 req/s. A cache hit takes 3 ms and a miss (from the DB) takes 80 ms. The hit ratio is 95%. What are the average latency and the DB queries/s?
mad2-w11-q10.explanation: Average = 0.95 × 3 + 0.05 × 80 = 2.85 + 4 = 6.85 ms. The DB sees only the misses: 2000 × 0.05 = 100 queries/s. Option A takes a plain average of the two latencies; option B counts the hits as DB queries; option C ignores the latency of the misses.

mad2-w11-q11.question: You need 50 posts and their authors (all different). How many queries go out with `selectinload(Post.author)` and with `joinedload(Post.author)` in SQLAlchemy?
mad2-w11-q11.explanation: `selectinload` runs 2 queries: first the posts, then all the authors at once with `WHERE id IN (...)`. `joinedload` brings everything in a single query with a JOIN. Option A is the lazy-loading (N+1) number; option C swaps the two; option D is an N+1-style count too.

mad2-w11-q12.question: An API runs at 300 req/s and each request holds a DB connection for its whole latency. The latency rises from 80 ms to 250 ms, and the pool has 40 connections. By Little's law, how many connections are needed at once before and after, and is the pool enough?
options: 3.75 and 1.2; the pool is always enough
24 and 75; fine before, now 40 is too few
2400 and 7500; the pool was never enough
mad2-w11-q12.explanation: L = λ × W, with W in seconds: 300 × 0.08 = 24, and 300 × 0.25 = 75. 24 < 40 was fine, but 75 > 40, so requests will queue for a connection and latency will climb further. Option A forgets to compare 75 with 40; option B divides λ by W; option D forgets to convert ms to seconds.

mad2-w11-q13.question: An endpoint has 20 response times (ms): 63, 40, 1200, 55, 72, 45, 90, 61, 50, 400, 42, 75, 58, 850, 47, 65, 52, 80, 60, 70. Using the nearest-rank method (position ⌈p/100 × n⌉ in the sorted list), what are p50, p95 and the mean?
mad2-w11-q13.explanation: Sort them: 40, 42, 45, 47, 50, 52, 55, 58, 60, 61, 63, ..., 90, 400, 850, 1200. p50: ⌈0.5 × 20⌉ = 10th = 61. p95: ⌈0.95 × 20⌉ = 19th = 850. Mean = 3475 ÷ 20 = 173.75: three slow requests pushed the mean to roughly three times the median. Option B takes the median as the average of the 10th and 11th (62) and p95 as the last value; option C takes the 18th value and uses the median as the mean; option D swaps the median and the mean.

mad2-w11-q14.question: Every order has a different customer, and both the `customer` and `items` relationships use the default lazy loading. (i) How many queries does this code send? (ii) How many after adding `options(selectinload(Order.customer), selectinload(Order.items))`?
mad2-w11-q14.explanation: Lazy loading: 1 query for the orders, then 1 for the customer and 1 for the items for each order: 1 + 20 + 20 = 41. `selectinload` runs one extra `IN (...)` query per relationship: orders + customers + items = 3. mad2-w11-q15.question: Two files are served with an ETag: file A with `Cache-Control: max-age=60`, file B with `Cache-Control: no-cache`. The user opens the page at t = 0 s (both came with 200), then again at t = 30 s and t = 90 s. The content never changed. After t = 0, how many requests reach the server in total, and with what status?
options: 0 requests, both come from the cache
mad2-w11-q15.explanation: A: at t = 30 it is still fresh (within 60 s), so it comes from the cache with no network. At t = 90 it is stale, so the browser revalidates with `If-None-Match`: 304. B: `no-cache` revalidates every time, a 304 at both t = 30 and t = 90. 1 + 2 = 3 requests in total, all 304 (no body). Option A assumes some requests bring the full body again; option B reads `no-cache` as "use the cache without asking"; option C assumes the stale A is also used without asking.

mad2-w12-q7.question: Where should a Flask app's JWT secret and database password be kept?
options: In environment variables (or a secret manager); not in code or git
As a constant in `app.py`, so every developer has it
In one of the Vue frontend's `.js` files, next to the API URL
In the README, so whoever deploys the app knows it
mad2-w12-q7.explanation: Secrets should come from environment variables (or a secret manager), so they do not leak into code or git history and each environment can have its own value. Options B and D hand them to anyone who can see the repo; option C ships them to every browser user.

mad2-w12-q8.question: What is the biggest benefit of an `api` client module in a Vue app (one that handles the base URL, the `Authorization` header, the `res.ok` check and 401s)?
options: Requests automatically get faster because the headers are cached
This logic is not repeated in every component; behaviour stays consistent
The need to configure CORS on the backend goes away completely
Server-side validation is no longer needed, the client checks everything
mad2-w12-q8.explanation: With headers, the `res.ok` check and 401 handling in one place, no component forgets a check, and a change (such as a new header) happens in a single file. It does not change speed (option A), CORS (option C) or server validation (option D).

mad2-w12-q9.question: How should users' passwords be stored in the database?
options: In plain text, so they can be sent back on forgot password
As a strong, slow password hash such as bcrypt or argon2
In the JWT payload, so they are verified with every request
mad2-w12-q9.explanation: bcrypt/argon2 are deliberately slow, one-way password hashes: even if the DB leaks, recovering a password is very expensive. Plain text and Base64 (just an encoding, easily reversed) hand over the password on a leak; and anyone can decode a JWT payload.

mad2-w12-q10.question: At peak 90 jobs arrive per minute and each job holds a worker process for 6 s. (i) At least how many workers are needed to stop the queue growing? (ii) With 50% headroom (round up)?
mad2-w12-q10.explanation: Arrival rate = 90 / 60 = 1.5 jobs/s. Little: 1.5 × 6 = 9 workers. Headroom: 9 × 1.5 = 13.5, rounded up = 14. Option C rounds 13.5 down; option B divides 90 by 6 (never turning per minute into per second); option A multiplies while mixing seconds and minutes.

mad2-w12-q11.question: The access token has expired and `GET /api/v1/projects` returns 401. In this course's frontend design, where and how is this best handled?
options: Each component checks for 401 itself after its `fetch`
In one place, the `api` client: clear the auth store and redirect to login
The server should send 200 and an empty list instead of 401
A router guard checks the token every 5 seconds and logs out on expiry
mad2-w12-q11.explanation: A 401 means the identity check failed; it can happen on any request, so handle it once in the central `api` client: reset the auth store and redirect to login (or get a new token with the refresh token). Option A is the very duplication we want to avoid; option C is the wrong status and hides the bug; option D is polling, which still does not handle a 401 on requests in between.

mad2-w12-q13.question: A worker pool runs two kinds of jobs: 120 email jobs per minute (1 s each) and 30 report jobs per minute (10 s each). At least how many worker processes are needed so the queue does not grow?
mad2-w12-q13.explanation: Little's law for each type: emails 120 / 60 = 2 per s × 1 s = 2; reports 30 / 60 = 0.5 per s × 10 s = 5. Total 2 + 5 = 7. Option A adds up the job counts (120 + 30); option B adds only the job times (1 + 10); option D counts only the reports.

mad2-w12-q15.question: `GET /api/v1/projects?page=1` returns only the projects the user is a member of. The Redis cache-aside key is `projects:page:1` (TTL 60 s). At t = 0 Asha makes the request (a miss; her projects are cached). At t = 10 s Bilal (whose projects are different) opens the same URL. What does Bilal get, and what is the fix?
options: Bilal's own projects, because every request checks the token first
A 401, because Asha's token is now stored in the cache entry
An empty list for Bilal, until the TTL runs out
Asha's projects (leak); the key needs the user id, e.g. `projects:u42:page:1`
mad2-w12-q15.explanation: The key has no user id, so at t = 10 s Bilal's request gets a cache hit and the API returns Asha's projects (within the TTL). The token check does let the request through, but the cached data belongs to another user. Fix: put everything the result depends on into the key, here the user id and the page. Option A assumes the auth check also fixes the cache; option B is wrong because the cache stores the response, not the token; option C has no basis.
